stories.title: Oil Prices Bounce Back Up as Sea Route Stays Risky
stories.headline_kid: A narrow sea passage that carries much of the world's oil is still risky, so oil prices went up instead of down.
summary: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow strip of sea between Iran and Oman. Imagine it as a busy highway, except instead of cars, it's giant ships carrying oil that countries all over the world need. A huge amount of the world's oil sails through this one narrow gap every single day.

Iran, working together with Oman, has said it might stop ships it considers 'unfriendly' from passing through, and fine any ship that breaks its new rules. This made oil buyers nervous, so the price of oil jumped up again on Friday.

Just a few days ago, people thought oil prices might fall because there was hope of a calm deal to reopen the strait safely for everyone. Now the situation has flipped, showing how fast things can change when countries disagree over something so important.

Oil prices matter because they affect the cost of petrol, bus and taxi rides, and even the price of goods shipped by sea. Singapore has almost no oil of its own, so when oil becomes more expensive elsewhere, it can affect prices here too.

lenses.me: If oil gets pricier, the Grab or taxi ride your family takes to school or tuition might cost a little more.
lenses.family: Your parents may notice higher prices when filling up the car, or when ordering things delivered by ship or lorry.
lenses.friends: Your friends' families who drive or take buses often might feel the same small pinch in their pockets.
lenses.nation: Singapore buys almost all its oil from other countries, so a shaky Strait of Hormuz can ripple through transport costs across the island.
lenses.world: It shows how one narrow stretch of sea, far from Singapore, can affect fuel prices and trade for countries everywhere.

stories.title: Weaker Rains Push Up Rice Prices in India
stories.headline_kid: Rice, a food many families eat every day, is becoming more expensive in parts of India because the rain needed to grow it didn't fall enough this year.
summary: In southern India, rice is like rice is to us here — a staple food eaten with almost every meal. But this year, the monsoon rains that farmers depend on to water their rice fields have been weaker than usual, because of a weather pattern called El Niño.

Weaker rain means farmers can't plant as much rice, so there is less rice to go around. When something becomes scarcer but people still want to buy it, its price usually goes up — and that is exactly what is happening now.

Families in southern India are already feeling the pinch, paying more at the market for a bag of rice than before. Experts are worried this could get worse if the rains stay weak for the rest of the season.

This matters to us in Singapore too. We import almost all our food, including rice, and some of it comes from India. If rice becomes pricier there, it could eventually mean slightly higher prices for rice-based dishes here, like biryani, thosai or nasi lemak.

lenses.me: Your favourite rice dish, like fried rice or biryani, might cost a little more at the hawker centre one day.
lenses.family: Your family's grocery bill could creep up slightly if rice imports become more expensive.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose families cook rice often at home might also notice the change in price.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies on imported food, so shortages in other countries can affect what we pay here.
lenses.world: It shows how weather changes in one country can affect food prices for people thousands of kilometres away.

stories.title: Singapore's Big Banks Report Higher Profits
stories.headline_kid: Two of Singapore's biggest banks, OCBC and UOB, made more money this quarter — even though interest rates are lower.
summary: OCBC and UOB are two of Singapore's largest banks — think of them like the big, trusted piggy banks that grown-ups use to save, borrow, and invest money. On Friday, both banks announced they made more profit in the last three months than before.

OCBC's profit jumped by 22 per cent, while UOB's rose by 10 per cent. A big reason for this was 'wealth management' — this is when banks help wealthy customers manage and grow their money, and the banks earn fees for this service.

This happened even though interest rates, the extra money banks earn from loans, have been falling. That usually squeezes bank profits, like a smaller allowance making it harder to save. But strong fee income helped make up the difference.

This is good news for Singapore's economy. Banks doing well often means the country's overall financial health is stable, which can affect things like jobs, loans for parents' businesses, and even the CPF savings many families rely on.

lenses.me: If your parents or relatives have savings or investments with these banks, this news is good for them.
lenses.family: Strong bank profits can mean more stable jobs in the banking sector, where many parents work.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose parents work in banks or finance might hear cheerful news at home this week.
lenses.nation: Healthy banks are a sign that Singapore's economy is holding up well, even during uncertain global times.
lenses.world: Singapore's banks are watched by other countries as an example of how financial hubs can stay strong.

stories.title: Meta Fined Huge Amount Over Harm to Teens Online
stories.headline_kid: A US court has ordered Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, to pay a massive fine because a judge said its apps hurt young people's mental health.
summary: Meta is the company that owns popular apps like Facebook and Instagram. A court in the US state of New Mexico ruled that Meta must pay $567 million (about S$730 million) and change how its apps work for young users.

The judge said Meta had designed its platforms in ways that made children addicted to scrolling, similar to how a game might be designed to keep you playing 'just one more round.' The state's top lawyer argued this harmed young users' mental health and wellbeing.

This case is part of a bigger, growing worry around the world about how social media affects children and teenagers — things like feeling anxious, comparing themselves to others online, or struggling to put their phone down.

Even though this happened in the US, it matters here too. Many Singaporean kids and teens use Instagram and Facebook, and rulings like this could push tech companies everywhere to build safer features for young users in future.

lenses.me: This might lead to new safety features on apps you or your older siblings use, like better time limits or content filters.
lenses.family: Parents may feel reassured that companies are being pushed to make apps safer for children.
lenses.friends: Your friends who use social media a lot might notice new safety pop-ups or limits appearing on their apps.
lenses.nation: Singapore's own online safety rules for children may be strengthened further as global pressure on tech companies grows.
lenses.world: This case could set an example for other countries to hold big tech companies responsible for protecting young users.

stories.title: Singapore Faces 'Wounded and Hungry' Indonesia in Crunch Match
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's football team is preparing for a huge match against Indonesia, who their coach says are 'wounded and hungry' for a win.
summary: Singapore's national football team is gearing up for an important match against Indonesia in the ASEAN Football Championship. This tournament is like the World Cup for Southeast Asian countries, and every match matters a lot.

Singapore's head coach, Gavin Lee, has been telling his players to stay calm and focused ahead of the big game. Staying calm under pressure is one of the toughest parts of playing sports at a high level.

On the other side, Indonesia's coach John Herdman described his team as 'wounded and hungry' — meaning they've had some tough losses recently but are determined to bounce back strongly against Singapore.

Matches like this bring the whole nation together, with fans cheering from home, void decks, and even school canteens. Win or lose, it's a chance for our players to show grit and teamwork on the big stage.
